claim: The widely-repeated market narrative (via Ben Thompson/Stratechery and the Dithering podcast) that Apple's Q2 2021 gross-margin jump (40% to 43% QoQ) was driven by the M1 chip transition is likely wrong; the actual driver was a services/hardware revenue mix shift.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin
scope_conditions: Apple fiscal Q2 2021 (calendar Q1 2021), company-wide gross margin
quoted_support: Apple's gross margins jumped to 43% from 40% in the prior quarter. ... The Dithering crew hypothesized that the shift to the M1 was a big enough jump to move Apple's margins up by $3 billion. This is probably not the case.

claim: In the same quarter, services revenue rose from 24% to 31% of Apple's gross profit while hardware fell from 76% to 69%; services margin rose from 68% to 70% while hardware margin rose only from 35% to 36% -- meaning the margin jump is explained mostly by mix shift toward high-margin services, not by silicon-driven hardware cost savings.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin
scope_conditions: Apple fiscal Q2 2021, hardware vs. services split (Apple-disclosed categories)
quoted_support: Hardware margins did increase slightly, from 35% to 36%, but services margins increased by more, 68% to 70%. In the recent quarter services revenue went from 24% of gross profits to 31% of gross profits, while hardware decreased from 76% to 69%.

claim: Digits to Dollars models the M1 transition's per-unit gross margin gain on Mac hardware at roughly 8 percentage points, based on Apple paying ~$25/chip to TSMC versus an assumed ~$100/chip previously paid to Intel, on a ~$1500 MacBook with a $960 cost of goods.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin (at the product level)
scope_conditions: Mac/MacBook only, author's own back-of-envelope model, explicitly caveated as containing 'a ton of simplifications and assumptions'
quoted_support: Apple probably pays TSMC about $25 per chip ... So they are increasing gross margins by 8 points ($75 in savings/$960 BOM).

claim: Despite an 8-point per-unit margin benefit from M1, the company-wide gross margin contribution from the M1 transition in the quarter analyzed was only about 0.3 percentage points (roughly $300 million), because only a partial share of that quarter's ~5 million MacBook shipments (about 4 million) had already transitioned to M1 -- directly rebutting the claim that M1 was worth $3 billion in a single quarter.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin (company-wide, near-term)
scope_conditions: Single quarter (Q2 FY2021), Mac-only impact scaled to whole-company gross margin
quoted_support: Apple probably sold about 5 million MacBooks last quarter, call it 4 million with the M1 ... which works out to $300 million in gross margin improvements, which means the shift to M1 contributed 0.3% (not 3%, 0.3%) of gross margin improvement in the quarter.

claim: Apple no longer discloses unit shipment volumes, forcing all third-party silicon-margin models (including this one) to rely on estimated unit counts, a structural data-availability constraint.
stance_target: Estimation-method caveat for Mac/iPhone margin figures
scope_conditions: Apple financial disclosure practice, ongoing since ~2018
quoted_support: Apple no longer breaks out their unit volumes ... (this would be a lot more fun if they still disclosed unit shipments)
